issues.legal_issue: A state acquisition of intermediary estates for agrarian reform serves a public purpose when it advances the interests of the community rather than the private interest of an individual.
material_facts: The legislation acquired intermediaries’ interests in estates and changed the land-tenure system, including by raising the status of cultivators and providing for village bodies and cooperative farming.

The acquired property was to vest in the State or village bodies subject to State supervision, and the scheme did not transfer particular property to an individual for that individual’s private purposes.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition served a public purpose, and the Act was not invalid for want of one.
issues.legal_principle: The meaning of “public purpose” is elastic and depends on the statute, the time, and society’s needs; the test is whether the acquisition serves the general interest of the community rather than an individual’s private interest. The Court applied this principle in interpreting the constitutional requirement in Article 31(2), while holding that the Act was protected from challenge under Articles 31(4), 31-A and 31-B.

predicates.state_acquires_intermediary_estates: The government acquires the interests of intermediaries in landed estates.
predicates.agrarian_reform_benefits_the_community: The acquisition forms part of a scheme to reform land tenure or improve the position of cultivators for the community’s benefit.
predicates.property_is_not_transferred_for_an_indiv: The acquired property is not taken to give it to an individual for that individual’s private purposes.

issues.definition: When the government acquires intermediaries’ estates as part of a community-benefiting agrarian reform, or does not transfer the property for an individual’s private use, the acquisition serves a public purpose.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge that estate-acquisition legislation provides inadequate or illusory compensation is barred when the legislation satisfies the constitutional conditions that protect it from such a challenge.
material_facts: The Act provided compensation calculated by reference to the net assets of the acquired estate and made compensation due from the date of vesting, with interest.
The Act provided for payment in cash, bonds, or a combination, and for determination of compensation by an officer with a right of appeal.
The Bill was pending when the Constitution came into force and received the President’s assent.
The appellants argued that compensation was inadequate, that non-income-producing property received no separate compensation, and that payment was left to the Government’s discretion.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the Act’s validity could not be challenged on the ground that it failed to provide compensation or provided inadequate compensation; it also rejected the contention that the compensation provisions made payment illusory.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 31(4), 31-A and 31-B barred the relevant challenge. Article 31-A did not repeal Part III; its proviso preserved the alternative application of Article 31(2), with the President as the decision-maker on compliance for a qualifying State law. The Court also relied on sections 27, 28, 65 and 68 of the Act, which made compensation obligatory and provided for its payment. It rejected the argument that the provisions left payment entirely to the Government’s discretion.

predicates.state_estate_acquisition_law: The challenged law provides for the State to acquire estates.
predicates.compensation_challenge_made: A person challenges the law on the ground that compensation is absent, inadequate, or illusory.
predicates.law_meets_constitutional_protection_cond: The law satisfies the constitutional conditions that protect it from a challenge based on fundamental rights.

issues.definition: If a protected state estate-acquisition law is challenged for providing absent, inadequate, or illusory compensation, the challenge is barred.

issues.legal_issue: A legislature may leave administrative details to the executive when the legislature itself has laid down the main principles governing the matter.
material_facts: The Act set out the main principles concerning the acquisition and compensation scheme.
It left details, including matters concerning interest and the form or timing of payment, to be prescribed by the executive.
issues.conclusion: The delegation was within permissible limits and did not delegate essential legislative power.
issues.legal_principle: The legislature may prescribe the governing principles and delegate matters of detail to rule-making authorities. The Court considered the Act’s provisions, including sections 6(e), 6(g) and 68, in light of the legislative powers concerning acquisition and compensation under List II, Entry 36 and List III, Entry 42.

predicates.legislature_sets_main_principles: The legislature itself establishes the principal rules governing the legislative scheme.
predicates.executive_is_left_only_administrative_de: The executive is authorized to prescribe implementation details rather than decide the scheme’s essential policy.

issues.definition: When the legislature establishes the scheme’s main principles and leaves only implementation details to the executive, the delegation is valid.

issues.legal_issue: Estate-acquisition legislation is not a fraud on the Constitution merely because earlier laws affecting landowners preceded it.
material_facts: The appellants relied on earlier provincial enactments and alleged that they were part of a plan to reduce landowners’ incomes before acquiring their estates.
The earlier enactments were passed before the Constitution came into force and were not shown to be connected with the acquisition legislation.
issues.conclusion: The Act was not a fraud on the Constitution on the basis of the earlier enactments relied upon.
issues.legal_principle: A fraud-on-the-Constitution allegation must be supported by facts connecting the impugned legislation to the asserted evasion; the earlier enactments identified in this case did not establish such a connection. The Court rejected the allegation and upheld the Act as a whole.

predicates.constitutional_fraud_claim: A person alleges that legislation was enacted as a device to evade constitutional limits.
predicates.claim_relies_on_prior_laws: The allegation relies on earlier enactments as evidence of the asserted device.
predicates.prior_laws_are_unconnected_to_the_acquis: The earlier enactments are not shown to be connected with the challenged acquisition scheme.

issues.definition: A fraud-on-the-Constitution claim based on earlier laws does not succeed when those laws are unconnected to the challenged acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: A Crown grant does not prevent a legislature with authority over the subject matter from legislating for compulsory acquisition of the granted property.
material_facts: Some appellants held landed estates under grants made by the former British Government.
The appellants argued that the grants and the legislation governing the estates made those properties immune from later acquisition legislation.
issues.conclusion: The granted estates were not immune from acquisition and stood on no higher footing than other property in the region.
issues.legal_principle: A Crown grant cannot deprive a competent legislature of legislative authority over property within its jurisdiction unless the Constitution expressly prohibits the legislation. The Court relied on the Privy Council decision in Thakur Jagannath Baksh Singh v. United Provinces, which rejected the proposition that a legislature is barred from legislating to vary the effect of a Crown grant.

predicates.property_is_held_under_a_crown_grant: The owner holds the property under a grant made by a former sovereign authority.
predicates.legislature_has_authority_over_the_prope: The legislature has constitutional authority to legislate about the property or its acquisition.
predicates.constitution_does_not_prohibit_the_acqui: No constitutional provision prohibits the legislature from acquiring the property.

issues.definition: A Crown grant does not prevent acquisition when the legislature has authority over the property and no constitutional prohibition applies.

issues.legal_issue: Property privately dedicated to charity is not immune from compulsory acquisition for a public purpose.
material_facts: Religious institutions held endowed properties whose income was used for religious or charitable purposes, including gatherings and feeding religious mendicants.
The Act acquired the estates and used the institutions’ net income as the basis for compensation.
issues.conclusion: The charitable dedication did not exempt the properties from compulsory acquisition.
issues.legal_principle: A private dedication to charity does not remove property from the sovereign’s power to acquire it for a public purpose. The Court also observed that the Act based compensation for the institutions on the net income derived from their properties.

predicates.property_is_privately_dedicated_to_chari: An owner has dedicated property to religious or charitable purposes.
predicates.state_acquires_property_for_public_purpo: The State compulsorily acquires the property for a public purpose.

issues.definition: A private charitable dedication does not prevent the State from acquiring property for a public purpose.

issues.legal_issue: A claim based on guarantees in a merger covenant does not prevent acquisition when the property is treated as private property and the dispute falls within the constitutional bar on judicial jurisdiction over covenant disputes.
material_facts: A ruler’s property had been identified under a merger covenant as private property, and the Act proceeded to acquire it while treating it as private property and providing compensation.
The ruler claimed that the property and its income were protected by the covenant and related constitutional guarantees.
The Government disputed the assertion that the privy purse had been fixed in reliance on the income from the property.
issues.conclusion: The covenant-based challenge failed; the Court held that Article 362 did not impose a legal obligation on the legislature and that Article 363 barred judicial jurisdiction over the dispute arising from the covenant.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that Article 362 did not impose a legally enforceable obligation on Parliament or a State Legislature and that Article 363 barred jurisdiction over disputes arising out of the covenant. It also reasoned that treating the property as private property and offering compensation recognized the ruler’s ownership.

predicates.acquisition_challenge_relies_on_merger_c: A person challenges an acquisition by relying on guarantees in a merger covenant.
predicates.property_is_treated_as_private_and_compe: The acquisition treats the property as private property and provides compensation for it.
predicates.dispute_arises_from_covenant: Resolving the claim would require deciding a dispute arising from the covenant.

issues.definition: A covenant-based acquisition challenge is barred when the property is treated as private, compensation is offered, and the dispute arises from the covenant.

issues.legal_issue: A court cannot infer a constitutional limitation from the supposed spirit of the Constitution when the relevant constitutional provisions expressly address the matter.
material_facts: The appellants argued that the Constitution’s spirit implied requirements of public purpose and compensation even though the impugned acquisition law was expressly protected from challenges under relevant constitutional provisions.
The Act concerned acquisition of estates, a subject addressed by express constitutional provisions.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected reliance on an implied constitutional spirit to invalidate the Act.
issues.legal_principle: Where the Constitution’s provisions are explicit, the Court cannot use an asserted spirit of the Constitution to impose a limitation that the text does not state. The Court applied Articles 31(4), 31-A and 31-B and reasoned that an implied limitation would conflict with their express terms.

predicates.constitutional_text_expressly_addresses_: The Constitution contains express provisions addressing the kind of acquisition or challenge in issue.
predicates.challenge_depends_on_an_unstated_limitat: The challenge depends on implying a limitation that is not stated in the constitutional text.

issues.definition: When express constitutional text addresses an issue, a challenge cannot succeed by relying on a contrary limitation inferred only from constitutional spirit.

issues.legal_issue: When the State acquires an entire estate and compensation is calculated by reference to its net income, the absence of separate compensation for non-income-producing parts does not by itself make the acquisition confiscatory.
material_facts: The Act acquired estates as wholes, including both income-producing and non-income-producing property.
Compensation was calculated by reference to the net income of the estate as a whole.
The appellants argued that particular non-income-producing property, including waste land, received no separate compensation.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition was not confiscatory merely because non-income-producing properties within the estates received no separate compensation.
issues.legal_principle: Where an entire estate is acquired and compensation is based on the net income of that estate, the estate’s non-income-producing components may be considered as part of the whole; the absence of separate compensation for those components does not alone make the legislation confiscatory. The Court contrasted this with a case in which separate pieces of property, rather than the estate as a whole, were acquired.

predicates.entire_estate_is_acquired: The State acquires the estate as a whole rather than selecting individual pieces of it.
predicates.compensation_is_based_on_estate_wide_net: The compensation calculation uses the net income of the estate as a whole.
predicates.some_estate_property_produces_no_income: Some property within the acquired estate does not itself produce income.

issues.definition: When an entire estate is acquired and compensation is based on its overall net income, non-income-producing components do not by themselves make the acquisition confiscatory.
